newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: U.S., South Korean defence ministers hold talks.
newsitem.headline: U.S., South Korean defence ministers hold talks.

text.p: The U.S. and South Korean defence ministers met on Thursday to discuss a food crisis causing near-famine in North Korea and to assess joint security against the heavily-armed communist state.
Talks between William Cohen and Kim Dong-jin came a day after a top North Korean army official said the North was "on the brink of war" that it did not want.
But analysts in Seoul and Tokyo noted after the broadcast speech by the chief general of the North Korean army on state-run Radio Pyongyang that the North had issued such warnings in the past.
Cohen told reporters on Wedesday that there had been no threatening military moves by the North.

He was due to fly by helicopter to the heavily-fortified Demilitarised Zone (DMZ) between the Koreas later on Thursday to meet some of the 37,000 U.S. troops stationed in the South as part of a joint defence against Pyongyang's 1.1 million-member military.
The secretary was to also hold talks with South Korean President Kim Young-sam and Foreign Minister Yoo Chong-ha.

Among issues on the agenda during Cohen's first visit to the Pacific as secretary were plans for food aid by South Korea, the United States and other countries to the North and expectations that near-famine will force Pyongyang to agree to four-way peace talks with South Korea, China and the United States.

"Hopefully, this will allow us to (go ahead) with the four-party talks in the near future," Cohen told reporters on Wednesday, adding that evidence was mounting that the food shortage in the North was very severe.

North Korea, which still has not made formal peace with the South more than four decades after the 1950-53 Korean War, reported to U.N. officials earlier that more than 100 children had already starved to death in the Stalinist state.
The North has told Washington and Seoul it will respond next week to their proposal for peace talks and expectations it will agree to attend, albeit with strings attached.
On Wednesday, Kim Yong-chun, chief of the general staff of the North Korean People's Army, accused Seoul and Washington of "war agitation."

"Our country's situation is on the brink of war, and the launching mechanism for a northward invasion is already in place," he told a rally in Pyongyang to mark the fourth anniversary of North Korean leader Kim Jong-il's appointment to chairman of the National Defence Committee.
"We do not want war, but we are not afraid of war. It is our sacred, independent right to take strong measures against those provoking war," Kim Yong-chun said.

On visits to Hawaii and Japan in recent days, Cohen predicted that virtually all of the 37,000 U.S. troops would remain in South Korea for the forseeable future, even if the Koreas made peace and were united.
He said they should remain as part of a stabilising force of 100,000 American troops in the western Pacific.

In another controversial remark, Cohen also warned that South Korea would be making a mistake if it bought Russian SA-12 anti-aircraft missiles because the arms could threaten U.S. air force jets in the confusion of any new conflict.
Cohen appeared to soften that stance on Wednesday, although he repeated that the South should buy U.S.-made Patriot air defence missiles because they were programmed to avoid targeting U.S. jets.
